title: In the liver of 13 mammals, a gene neighbourhood with more DNA carries more enhancer marks, at 0.45 to 0.7 of the proportional rate, and the increase is in DNA not shared between the species
abstract: When one mammal has more non-coding DNA than another in the same gene neighbourhood, it also has more liver enhancer marks there, at about half to three quarters of the rate expected if marks were spread evenly over the DNA; all of the increase is in DNA that does not align between the two species. This matters because counts of marked elements, such as enhancers per gene, are used as measures of regulatory function, but a large part of such a count follows the plain amount of DNA. We used published liver ChIP-seq peaks (H3K27ac and H3K4me3) of 13 mammals and matched the same gene neighbourhoods across species: the DNA between two adjacent orthologous genes, or the introns of one gene. The elasticity is the percent change of the peak count for a 1% change of DNA length (0: count independent of DNA amount; 1: count proportional to DNA amount). Whole-genome alignments let us keep only windows whose two copies contain the same DNA. In these windows, the random-effects mean elasticity of enhancer marks (H3K27ac without H3K4me3) over 12 human-versus-species comparisons was 0.45 (95% CI 0.21-0.70) with young repeats removed, and 0.69 (0.51-0.87) in windows that also keep every human conserved element. Peaks in DNA that aligns between the two windows did not follow length (-0.07, -0.27 to 0.12); peaks in unaligned DNA did (0.75, 0.60-0.89), and unaligned DNA had 0.44 (0.39-0.50) times the mark density of aligned DNA. Without alignment checks the estimates were inflated (0.72 between genes, 0.90 in introns), and conserved elements themselves appeared to scale (0.71 in introns). Pairwise estimates were low for close species pairs, which may reflect short-read mappability and length error. Liver RNA-seq could not show whether the marks that follow DNA amount change expression. Similar patterns were reported before in other designs; our contribution is the within-neighbourhood estimate, the aligned/unaligned split, and the size of the artefact. Limits: 50-bp reads on 2013 assemblies, orthology by gene name, one tissue, and marks are not proof of function. A laboratory can test whether marked elements in lineage-specific DNA change target-gene expression less often than marked elements in shared DNA.

display.caption: A: Observed peak counts divided by the counts expected if a window's count did not depend on its length, against the within-window deviation of DNA length across species. Blue: enhancer peaks, all matched intergenic windows. Green: enhancer peaks in the strictest windows (clean alignment, every conserved element kept), young repeats removed. Orange: human conserved elements (control). Dashed line: count proportional to DNA. B: Multi-species elasticity estimates (95% CI) for each filter step, H3K4me3 peaks and controls; random placement per base recovers 0.96.

A: Elasticity in human-vs-species window pairs, split by where the peak lies: peaks in aligned DNA do not follow window length; peaks in unaligned DNA carry the increase. B: Enhancer-mark density in unaligned DNA relative to aligned DNA, per species and the mean of 12 species (95% CI). C: Share of each species' liver enhancer peaks that are shared with human, lie in aligned DNA not marked in human, or lie in DNA not aligned to human.

A: Elasticity for each species pair against divergence time in clean windows (blue, 78 pairs; rising trend) and the strictest windows (green, 77 pairs; no trend), with precision-weighted trend lines; intervals clipped at the axis. B: Expression test: the link between liver expression and the part of the enhancer count that follows DNA amount, relative to all count change (IV/OLS, bootstrap 95% CI). The designs disagree, so the test is inconclusive.
